descs.t: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race, and appeared with him at a Detroit church days before Tuesday's vote. She lost the primary to El-Sayed with 47.55% and first endorsed him. We go through what she said, how both campaigns reacted, and what the polls show.

Haley Stevens crossed party lines to back Mike Rogers for the Michigan Senate seat, saying she cannot stand with hate. Democrats from Michigan to Washington are calling it betrayal, while El-Sayed's campaign says it raised $1.2 million in four hours. We look at why she did it and whether it changes Tuesday's result.

A Democrat who lost the Michigan primary to Abdul El-Sayed now says her vote goes to Republican Mike Rogers, and she said it standing beside him: we cannot stand with hate. Her own party is in revolt and Trump says he would love to have her. We break down the fallout and what it means for the fight for the Senate.

intro.plain: Big turn in Michigan. Democrat Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, just endorsed the Republican, Mike Rogers, and stood next to him at a Detroit church. Her party is furious, Trump is praising her, and the vote is Tuesday. So tell me in the chat: does an endorsement like this move any votes at all?
intro.mid: Haley Stevens just did what almost no Democrat does: she endorsed the Republican in a Senate race days before the vote. Her reason, in her words, we cannot stand with hate. El-Sayed's camp says it raised $1.2 million in four hours off the back of it. Chat, is this principle or payback for a lost primary?
intro.bold: A Democrat just stood next to Mike Rogers and said her vote goes to him, not to her own party's nominee, Abdul El-Sayed. We cannot stand with hate, she said. Her party is calling her a traitor and Trump wants her in the GOP. So I want to hear it from you in the chat: betrayal, or the bravest move of the cycle?

hook.plain: A Democrat who lost the Michigan primary just endorsed the Republican, days before the vote. Here is what she said and why her party is in uproar.
hook.mid: She endorsed him after the primary. Now she stands next to his Republican rival. Here is why Haley Stevens switched, and what it could do on Tuesday.
hook.bold: We cannot stand with hate. That is how Haley Stevens explained backing a Republican over her own party's nominee. Here is the fallout.

descs.t: A new YouGov poll of 2,141 likely voters, taken October 26 to 29, has Democrat James Talarico at 51% and Republican Ken Paxton at 47% in the Texas Senate race. Early vote tracking puts total votes at 7,705,786 as of November 1, about 74.1% of projected turnout. We walk through the numbers and what they mean for Tuesday.

Ken Paxton trails James Talarico 47 to 51 in YouGov's latest Texas Senate poll, with roughly three quarters of the expected vote already cast. Some voters on the right say they are crossing over, while Paxton's backers attack Talarico on taxes, borders and gender. We break down why a Republican is struggling in Texas and whether the poll holds.

Texas has a Democrat ahead in the Senate race in YouGov's final poll. A split on the right and a huge early vote could make this the shock of election night. We go through the numbers, the attacks and what could still change.

intro.plain: Let's look at Texas. YouGov's new poll of 2,141 likely voters has James Talarico at 51% and Ken Paxton at 47% in the Senate race. And early voting is huge: over 7.7 million votes, about 74.1% of the projected turnout, already cast. Chat, do you believe this poll, or does Paxton hold Texas on Tuesday?
intro.mid: Texas is close. YouGov has Democrat James Talarico up four on Ken Paxton, 51 to 47, and three quarters of the expected vote is already in. Some voters on the right are telling reporters they will cross over. Chat, is Paxton the reason Republicans could lose Texas, or is this poll wrong?
intro.bold: A Democrat leading a Senate race in Texas. YouGov has James Talarico at 51 and Ken Paxton at 47, with 7.7 million votes already cast. Paxton's own side is split. Chat, straight question: if Texas sends a Democrat to the Senate, who is to blame?
